nodes.title: Aims of time series analysis
Time series decomposition
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{TIME SERIES DECOMPOSITION}}

View $Y_t$ as composed of: a \textbf{Trend}, a \textbf{Seasonal} comp., a \textbf{cycle}, and an \textbf{Erratic} comp.

\textbf{Additive}: $Y_t = T_t + S_t + C_t + E_t$

\textbf{Multiplicative}: $Y_t = T_t \cdot S_t \cdot C_t \cdot E_t$

note $\log$ transforms a multiplicative decomposition into an additive one

\textbf{Diagnostic:} if the seasonal swing grows with the level of the series, prefer the multiplicative form (or model $\log Y_t$ additively).

nodes.title: Fitting a trend
Fitting a seasonal component
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FITTING A SEASONAL COMPONENT}}

For $Y_t = S_t + E_t$ (purely seasonal, no trend; assume mean zero, $\bar{y}_t = 0$):

\textbf{1. Seasonal factors.} For monthly data introduce $\alpha_{\text{Jan}}, \alpha_{\text{Feb}}, \dots, \alpha_{\text{Dec}}$ with $\sum_m \alpha_m = 0$:
\[ y_t = \alpha_{\text{month}(t)} + E_t. \]

Note they can always sum to 0, just change the intercept of the model (the level of the trend)

\textbf{2. Moving averages.} For monthly data, $\mathrm{MA}(12)$:
\[ y_t^{\text{deseason.}} = \frac{0.5\, y_{t-6} + y_{t-5} + \dots + y_{t+5} + 0.5\, y_{t+6}}{12}. \]

nodes.title: How to assign the Probability law of the process
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{HOW TO ASSIGN THE PROBABILITY LAW OF THE PROCESS}}



Defining a \textbf{statistical model} for a stoch.\ process requires specifying its probabilty law. 

\begin{keydef}
\textbf{Probability law of a stochastic process.} It is uniquely specified by the joint density of $(Y_{t_1}, \dots, Y_{t_n})$ (the FDDs):
\[ p_{t_1, \dots, t_n}(y_1, \dots, y_n) = P\bigl(Y_{t_1} \le y_1, \dots, Y_{t_n} \le y_n\bigr), \]
for every integer $n \ge 1$ and every tuple of times $(t_1, \dots, t_n) \in T^n$.
\end{keydef}                   
                                           


\emph{Concrete example of one FDD.} Take $n = 4$ and times $(t_1, t_2, t_3, t_4) = (1, 10, 70, 106)$. The corresponding FDD is the joint density
\[ p_{1,10,70,106}(y_1, y_{10}, y_{70}, y_{106}) \;=\; P\bigl(Y_1 \le y_1,\, Y_{10} \le y_{10},\, Y_{70} \le y_{70},\, Y_{106} \le y_{106}\bigr), \]
i.e.\ how the process values at times $1, 10, 70, 106$ are jointly distributed. The full law of the process requires knowing this kind of joint for \emph{every} choice of $n$ and times --- this is the \emph{family} we feed into Kolmogorov.

By Kolmogorov's extension theorem, any consistent family of FDDs (i.e.\ marginalisation and         
permutation invariance hold) determines a unique probability law on the path space.

Basically, you want to know
- The margianl at every t eg $Y_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_t, \sigma_t^2)$ for each $t$. 
- The bivariate densities $p_{s,t}(y_s, y_t)$ capturing dependences eg $\mathrm{Cov}(Y_s, Y_t) = 0$ for $s \neq t$ gives an iid process (under some assumptions); $\mathrm{Cov}(Y_s, Y_t) = \sigma^2 \rho^{|t-s|}$ gives an AR(1)-like correlation. Note that from knowing the densities you cannot know the bivariates! (if x distributes in a way, y in another, what is the joint? depends on correlation)

nodes.title: Forecasting algorithms — Cases 0, 1, 2 (SES / Holt / Holt-Winters)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FORECASTING ALGORITHMS — CASES 0, 1, 2}}

Predict $y_{t+1}\mid y_{1:t}$ — often the ultimate goal. At time $t$ define the \textbf{forecast function}\[ f_t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad f_t(h) = \hat y_{t+h\mid t}, \]i.e.\ $f_t(h)$ is the $h$-step-ahead forecast made using information up to $t$.


The formulas belwo actually derive from SSM ! 

\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
 & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Case 0 (SES)}} \textit{(no trend, no seasonality)} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Case 1 — Holt}} \textit{(add trend)} & \textbf{\textcolor{red}{Case 2 — Holt-Winters}} \textit{(add seasonality)} \\
\textbf{Forecast} $\hat y_{t+h\mid t}$ & $\hat y_{t+h\mid t} = L_t$ \;\textit{(flat)} & $\hat y_{t+h\mid t} = L_t + h\, B_t$ \;\textit{(level + slope $\times h$)} & $\hat y_{t+h\mid t} = L_t + h\, B_t + S_{t+h-m}$ \;\textit{(level + slope + seasonal at matching period)} \\
\textbf{State} $L_t$ \textit{(level)} & $L_t = \alpha\, y_t + (1-\alpha)\, L_{t-1}$ & $L_t = \alpha\, y_t + (1-\alpha)\,(L_{t-1} + B_{t-1})$ — \textit{use best yesterday prediction} & $L_t = \alpha\,(y_t - S_{t-m}) + (1-\alpha)\,(L_{t-1} + B_{t-1})$ — \textit{avoid double counting} \\
\textbf{State} $B_t$ \textit{(slope)} & — & $B_t = \beta\,(L_t - L_{t-1}) + (1-\beta)\, B_{t-1}$ — \textit{B is the average change in the last day and in the past} & $B_t = \beta\,(L_t - L_{t-1}) + (1-\beta)\, B_{t-1}$ \\
\textbf{State} $S_t$ \textit{(seasonal)} & — & — & $S_t = \gamma\,(y_t - L_{t-1} - B_{t-1}) + (1-\gamma)\, S_{t-m}$ --- \textit{S is the average of this period's seasonal deviation (today's observation minus the predicted non-seasonal part $L_{t-1} + B_{t-1}$) and the seasonal factor one full cycle ago $S_{t-m}$} \\
\textbf{Recursive form of} $\hat y$ & substitute $\hat y_{t\mid t-1} = L_{t-1}$ into the state update: $\hat y_{t+1\mid t} = \alpha\, y_t + (1-\alpha)\, \hat y_{t\mid t-1}$ & $\hat y_{t+1\mid t} = L_t + B_t = \alpha\, y_t + (1-\alpha)\, \hat y_{t\mid t-1} + B_t$ & $\hat y_{t+1\mid t} = L_t + B_t + S_{t+1-m} = \alpha\, y_t + (1-\alpha)\, \hat y_{t\mid t-1} + B_t + (S_{t+1-m} - S_{t-m})$ \\
\textbf{Forecast-error correction} & $\hat y_{t+1\mid t} = \hat y_{t\mid t-1} + \alpha\,(y_t - \hat y_{t\mid t-1})$ & — & — \\
\hline
\end{tabular}


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{$L_t$ and exponential smoothing.}} The simplest forecast is just a \emph{weighted average of past observations with geometrically decreasing weights} (not a regression --- the weight parameter $\alpha$ is fixed, not estimated): \[ \underbrace{\hat y_{t+1\mid t}}_{L_t} \;=\; \alpha\, y_t \;+\; \underbrace{\alpha(1-\alpha)\, y_{t-1} \;+\; \alpha(1-\alpha)^2\, y_{t-2} \;+\; \dots \;+\; \alpha(1-\alpha)^{t-1}\, y_1}_{(1 - a) \hat y_{t-1\mid t-2 = L_{t-1} } } , \qquad 0 < \alpha < 1, \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \alpha\,  (1-\alpha)^k \underbrace{=}_{t \to \infty}\; 1.\]

You can always apply this to compute Lt, but it will be correct only in he Case 0

nodes.title: Summaries of a stochastic process
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{SUMMARIES OF A STOCHASTIC PROCESS}}

For a single random variable $X$, the basic summaries are $\mathbb{E}[X]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)$. For a stochastic process $(Y_t)_{t \ge 1}$ these become \emph{functions of time} (and pairs of times):

$\bullet$ \textbf{Mean function}  $\mu : t \mapsto \mu(t) = \mathbb{E}[Y_t],  t = 1, 2, \dots$

$\bullet$ \textbf{Variance function}  $\sigma^2 : t \mapsto \sigma^2(t) = \mathrm{Var}(Y_t),  t = 1, 2, \dots$

$\bullet$ \textbf{Autocovariance function}  $\gamma : (t, t') \mapsto \gamma(t, t') = \mathrm{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t'}) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[(Y_t - \mu(t))(Y_{t'} - \mu(t'))\right],  t, t' = 1, 2, \dots$

$\bullet$ \textbf{Autocorrelation function}  $\rho : (t, t') \mapsto \rho(t, t') = \dfrac{\gamma(t, t')}{\sqrt{\sigma^2(t)\, \sigma^2(t')}} \in [-1, 1],  t, t' = 1, 2, \dots$

\textit{Consistency check:} $\gamma(t, t) = \sigma^2(t)$ and $\rho(t, t) = 1$.

Stationarity does not imply strict stat.

nodes.title: Strict stationarity
Ex.1 Most trivial example of stoch. process
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MOST TRIVIAL EXAMPLE OF STOCH.\ PROCESS}}

Say $Y_t,\ t \ge 0$ are independent. If, additionally, $Y_t$ have a common distribution (i.i.d.) with $p$:
\[ p_n(y_1,\dots,y_n) = p(y_1)\, p(y_2) \cdots p(y_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i). \]

If only indep.\ (not necessarily identically distrib.):
\[ p_n(y_1,\dots,y_n) = p_1(y_1)\, p_2(y_2) \cdots p_n(y_n). \]


\textbf{Example} Independent trials $Y_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}$ Bernoulli$(p)$.

Transition matrix:
\[ \begin{array}{c|cc} t-1 \backslash t & 0 & 1 \\ \hline 0 & 1-p & p \\ 1 & 1-p & p \end{array} \]

\textit{(rows identical: independence!)}

Both assume independence: irrealistic for time series

nodes.title: Introducing correlation — full dependence
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{INTRODUCING CORRELATION (DEPENDENCE)}}

\textbf{Step 1 — Full dependence (general chain rule).}\[ p_n(y_1, \dots, y_n) = p(y_1)\, p(y_2 \mid y_1)\, p(y_3 \mid y_1, y_2) \cdots p(y_n \mid y_1, \dots, y_{n-1}) = p(y_1) \prod_{t=2}^{n} p(y_t \mid y_1, \dots, y_{t-1}). \]This is fully general — no assumption made. The cost is that each conditional $p(y_t \mid y_1, \dots, y_{t-1})$ depends on the \emph{entire} past, so we have $n-1$ growing-dimension conditionals to specify or estimate. Infeasible in practice.

nodes.title: Example 2: categorical time series (state is observed)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 2 — CATEGORICAL TIME SERIES (PANEL ON VOTE INTENTION)}}

Anderson \& Goodman (1957) — panel study on US vote intention, May–October 1940 (6 monthly interviews). For each individual, $Y_t \in \mathcal{Y} = \{1, 2, 3\}$ with $1 = \text{Republican}$, $2 = \text{Democrat}$, $3 = \text{Don't know}$.

\textbf{Assumption:} $(Y_t)$ is a \textbf{homogeneous Markov chain}, i.e.\ (i) the vote intention $Y_t$ depends on the past only through $Y_{t-1}$ (Markov property), and (ii) the transition probabilities are constant over time.

\textbf{Transition matrix} (given as data for the exercises):

\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
$t-1 \;\backslash\; t$ & $1$ (Rep.) & $2$ (Dem.) & $3$ (Don't know) \\
\hline
$1$ (Rep.)        & $0.6$ & $0.3$ & $0.1$ \\
$2$ (Dem.)        & $0.1$ & $0.7$ & $0.2$ \\
$3$ (Don't know)  & $0.0$ & $0.4$ & $0.6$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}

\textit{Initial state:} at $t = 0$, the person is undecided, $Y_0 = 3$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Worked exercises}}

\textbf{(a) Probability that at $t = 1$ she expresses a preference for the Democrat Party.}\[ P(Y_1 = 2 \mid Y_0 = 3) = p_{3,2} = 0.4. \]
\textbf{(b) Probability that at $t = 1$ she is still undecided and at $t = 2$ she expresses a preference for the Democrat Party.}\[ P(Y_1 = 3,\ Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_0 = 3) = P(Y_1 = 3 \mid Y_0 = 3)\, P(Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_1 = 3) = p_{3,3}\, p_{3,2} = 0.6 \times 0.4 = 0.24. \]

\textbf{(c) Probability that she expresses a preference for the Democrat Party at $t = 2$.}\[ P(Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_0 = 3) = \sum_{k=1}^{3} P(Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_1 = k)\, P(Y_1 = k \mid Y_0 = 3) = \sum_{k=1}^{3} p_{k,2}\, p_{3,k} = 0.52. \]
\textbf{(d) Given that she expresses a preference for the Democrat Party at $t = 2$, probability that she was still undecided at $t = 1$.}

\emph{Generic rule.} For any events $A$ and $B$ (with $P(B) > 0$),\[ P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}. \]Basically: the probability that $A$ and $B$ happen together, given that $B$ has happened.

With an extra event $C$ held fixed in the background the same rule reads\[ P(A \mid B,\, C) = \frac{P(A \cap B \mid C)}{P(B \mid C)}. \]

\emph{In our case:} take $A = \{Y_1 = 3\}$, $B = \{Y_2 = 2\}$, $C = \{Y_0 = 3\}$. Then\[ P\bigl(\underbrace{Y_1 = 3}_{A} \,\big|\, \underbrace{Y_2 = 2}_{B},\ \underbrace{Y_0 = 3}_{C}\bigr) = \frac{P\bigl(\underbrace{Y_1 = 3,\ Y_2 = 2}_{A \cap B} \mid \underbrace{Y_0 = 3}_{C}\bigr)}{P\bigl(\underbrace{Y_2 = 2}_{B} \mid \underbrace{Y_0 = 3}_{C}\bigr)}. \]

The numerator is exactly exercise (b) ($= 0.24$) and the denominator is exactly exercise (c) ($= 0.52$), so\[ P(Y_1 = 3 \mid Y_2 = 2,\ Y_0 = 3) = \frac{0.24}{0.52} \approx 0.4615. \]

\textbf{(e1, e2) Full distribution of $Y_2$ and $Y_3$, given $Y_0 = 3$ --- unified view.}

\emph{One-step recursion.} For any homogeneous Markov chain, the marginal distribution propagates by right-multiplication by $\mathbf{P}$:
\[ \boldsymbol\pi_{n+1} \;=\; \boldsymbol\pi_n\, \mathbf{P} \]
Both (e1) and (e2) are instances at consecutive steps. Initial datum: $Y_0 = 3$ deterministically.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(e1) Distribution of $Y_2$.}} 
In matrix-vector form $\boldsymbol\pi_2 = \boldsymbol\pi_1\, \mathbf{P}$. As you started from  $Y_0 = 3$, you have that $\pi_1$ = $(0,\, 0.4,\, 0.6)$
\[ \boldsymbol\pi_2 \;=\; (0,\, 0.4,\, 0.6) \begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ 0.1 & 0.7 & 0.2 \\ 0.0 & 0.4 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix} \;=\; (\underbrace{0.04}_{P(Y_2 = 1 \mid Y_0 = 3)},\, \underbrace{0.52}_{P(Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_0 = 3)},\, \underbrace{0.44}_{P(Y_2 = 3 \mid Y_0 = 3)}). \]
If this makes you feel better...
$\bullet$ $P(Y_2 = 1 \mid Y_0 = 3) = p_{1,1}\, p_{3,1} + p_{2,1}\, p_{3,2} + p_{3,1}\, p_{3,3} = 0.6 \cdot 0 + 0.1 \cdot 0.4 + 0 \cdot 0.6 = 0.04$.

$\bullet$ $P(Y_2 = 2 \mid Y_0 = 3) = p_{1,2}\, p_{3,1} + p_{2,2}\, p_{3,2} + p_{3,2}\, p_{3,3} = 0.3 \cdot 0 + 0.7 \cdot 0.4 + 0.4 \cdot 0.6 = 0.52$ (matches (c)).

$\bullet$ $P(Y_2 = 3 \mid Y_0 = 3) = p_{1,3}\, p_{3,1} + p_{2,3}\, p_{3,2} + p_{3,3}\, p_{3,3} = 0.1 \cdot 0 + 0.2 \cdot 0.4 + 0.6 \cdot 0.6 = 0.44$.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(e2) Distribution of $Y_3$.}} 

In matrix-vector form $\boldsymbol\pi_3 = \boldsymbol\pi_2\, \mathbf{P}$:
\[ \boldsymbol\pi_3 \;=\; (0.04,\, 0.52,\, 0.44) \begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ 0.1 & 0.7 & 0.2 \\ 0.0 & 0.4 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix} \;=\; (0.076,\, 0.552,\, 0.372). \]

nodes.title: Ergodic properties of a Markov chain (Theorem 2.1)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{ERGODIC PROPERTIES OF A MARKOV CHAIN}}

In general the random variables $Y_n$ are \emph{not} identically distributed — the distribution of $Y_n$ varies with $n$, hence the process $(Y_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is not (strictly) stationary. We want to study its \textbf{asymptotic behaviour} as $n \to \infty$. Remark: not about transition probabilities, they are fixed in standard HMM. This is the density distribution at each t. 


\begin{keydef}
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Theorem 2.1 (ergodicity).}} Let $(Y_t)$ be an \textbf{irreducible} and \textbf{aperiodic} Markov chain with finite state space $\mathcal{Y} = \{1, \dots, N\}$. Then:

\textbf{(1)} The conditional distribution $P(Y_n = \cdot \mid Y_0 = j)$ given initial state $j$ converges to a limit distribution $p^*(\cdot)$, independent of $j$:
\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} P(Y_n = k \mid Y_0 = j) = p^*(k) > 0, \qquad \forall j, k \in \mathcal{Y}, \qquad \sum_{k \in \mathcal{Y}} p^*(k) = 1. \]
\textbf{(2)} The limit $p^*$ satisfies the fixed-point equation
\[ \underbrace{p^*(k)}_{\text{prob.\ of being in } k \text{ (next step)}} \;=\; \sum_{i \in \mathcal{Y}} \underbrace{p^*(i)}_{\text{prob.\ of being in } i \text{ (current step)}} \cdot \underbrace{p_{i,k}}_{\text{transition } i \to k}, \qquad \forall k \in \mathcal{Y}. \]
In row-vector form: $\boldsymbol{p}^* = \boldsymbol{p}^* \, \mathbf{P}$.
\end{keydef}

*remark: we do not use f ( a < y < b) because up to know the statespace is finite 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{In words.}} Theorem 2.1 means that, at the limit, $Y_n$ is distributed according to the discrete law\[ Y_n \;\stackrel{d}{\to}\; \begin{cases} 1 & \text{with probability } p^*(1), \\ 2 & \text{with probability } p^*(2), \\ \;\vdots & \;\vdots \\ N & \text{with probability } p^*(N), \end{cases} \]i.e.\ $Y_n$ becomes (approximately, for large $n$) a categorical random variable on $\{1, \dots, N\}$ with probabilities $p^*(1), p^*(2), \dots, p^*(N)$ — regardless of the starting state $Y_0$.


\textit{Understanding (2):}

\textbf{(a) Always-true one-step update (law of total probability).} For \emph{any} sequence of distributions $\boldsymbol\pi_n$ produced by the chain,\[ \underbrace{\boldsymbol\pi_{n+1}(k)}_{\text{next-step prob.}} \;=\; \sum_{i \in \mathcal{Y}} \underbrace{\boldsymbol\pi_n(i)}_{\text{current prob.}} \cdot \underbrace{p_{i,k}}_{\text{transition } i \to k}, \]i.e.\ $\boldsymbol\pi_{n+1} = \boldsymbol\pi_n\, \mathbf{P}$. This is just LTP.

\textbf{(b) Fixed-point (stationarity) equation.} Set $\boldsymbol\pi_{n+1} = \boldsymbol\pi_n = \boldsymbol p$ in (a) — i.e.\ ask which distributions stay unchanged after one step:\[ \underbrace{p(k)}_{\text{same on both sides}} \;=\; \sum_{i \in \mathcal{Y}} p(i)\, p_{i,k}, \qquad \text{i.e.\ } \boldsymbol p = \boldsymbol p\, \mathbf{P}. \]
**So basically we are saying, you apply transition porbabilitis, you trasform to the next state, but the marginal probability is the same as t-1.** Note that hsi implies homogeneity in transition probabilities!!!

This is a \textbf{constraint}: it is \emph{not} satisfied by most distributions. The set of distributions for which it holds is exactly the set of \textbf{stationary / invariant} distributions of the chain — fixed points of the one-step map $\boldsymbol\pi \mapsto \boldsymbol\pi\, \mathbf{P}$.

Note that since the limit distribution is stationary, we can also prove its uniqueness (we're not jumpting aroudn at the limit!). 


\emph{Concrete check (2-state chain $\mathbf{P} = (\begin{smallmatrix} 0.8 & 0.2 \\ 0.4 & 0.6 \end{smallmatrix}))$.} Take $\boldsymbol\pi = (0.5,\,0.5)$: applying (a), $\boldsymbol\pi\,\mathbf{P} = (0.6,\,0.4) \neq \boldsymbol\pi$ — so it is \emph{not} a fixed point. Take instead $\boldsymbol p^* = (2/3,\,1/3)$: $\boldsymbol p^*\,\mathbf{P} = (2/3,\,1/3) = \boldsymbol p^*$ — fixed point, hence stationary. Theorem 2.1 part (2) says the limit $p^*$ is a fixed point of $\mathbf{P}$.





\textit{Remark.} If $P(Y_n = k \mid Y_0 = j) \to p^*(k)$ independently of $j$, then the marginal $P(Y_n = k)$ converges to the same limit! Hence, it is enough to study the asymptotic behaviour of the conditional distribution $P(Y_n = k \mid Y_0 = j)$ — results for the marginal $P(Y_n = k)$ then follow automatically.

nodes.title: Conditions of Theorem 2.1 — recurrent / aperiodic / irreducible
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{CONDITIONS OF THEOREM 2.1 — RECURRENT, APERIODIC, IRREDUCIBLE}}

Fix a state $j$ and consider the Markov chain started at $Y_0 = j$. Let
\[ f_j \;=\; P(\text{the chain ever returns to state } j \mid Y_0 = j). \]

\textbf{Recurrence / transience.}
$\bullet$ \textbf{Recurrent}: $f_j = 1$ --- the chain is certain to revisit $j$. Equivalently, the expected number of visits to $j$ is infinite (visits happen infinitely often almost surely).
$\bullet$ \textbf{Transient}: $f_j < 1$ --- there is a positive probability $1 - f_j$ of \emph{never} returning. The number of visits to $j$ is geometric with mean $1/(1 - f_j) < \infty$ --- finitely many visits a.s., and then the chain wanders off forever. The extreme case $f_j = 0$ (leaves at time $1$ and never comes back) is a degenerate sub-case of transience.
$\bullet$ \textbf{Positive recurrent} (a.k.a.\ \emph{recurrent non-null}): $f_j = 1$ \emph{and} the mean recurrence time (expected number of steps to return) is finite. This is what Theorem 2.1 needs.


\textbf{Periodicity.} 
State $j$ has \textbf{period $d$} if a return to $j$ is possible only at multiples of $d$ steps (and $d$ is the largest such integer). If $d = 1$ --- e.g.\ at least one self-loop $p_{j,j} > 0$, or returns possible at coprime lengths --- state $j$ is \textbf{aperiodic}.

\textbf{Closed set / irreducibility.}
A set $C \subseteq \mathcal{Y}$ is \textbf{closed} if no onestep transition is possible from any state inside $C$ to any state outside $C$:\[ p_{j,k} = 0 \quad \text{whenever } j \in C \text{ and } k \notin C. \] A Markov chain is \textbf{irreducible} if there are no (proper) closed sets --- equivalently, every state is reachable from every other state in finitely many steps.

\emph{Example (reducible chain).} On $\mathcal{Y} = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$,
\[ \mathbf{P} = \begin{pmatrix} 1/3 & 0 & 2/3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/4 & 0 & 3/4 \\ 1/2 & 0 & 1/2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/2 & 0 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix} \]
is reducible: the two sets $C_1 = \{1, 3\}$ and $C_2 = \{2, 4\}$ are each closed (no row in $C_1$ has positive mass on a column in $C_2$, and vice versa). The chain has no common limit distribution --- the long-run behaviour depends on which basin you start in.

\textbf{Consequences for an irreducible chain.}


$\bullet$ \emph{Class property.} All states share the same recurrence status: either all recurrent, or all transient. Idea: If $j$ and $k$ are mutually reachable and $j$ is recurrent, then starting at $k$ the chain reaches $j$ a.s., from $j$ it returns to $k$ infinitely often a.s.\ via the same argument, so $k$ is recurrent too. Note being irreducible this expans to all states.

$\bullet$ \emph{Finite state space.} If $|\mathcal{Y}| < \infty$, at least one state is visited infinitely often (pigeonhole). By the class property, \emph{all} states are positive recurrent. This guarantees the strict positivity $p^*(k) > 0$ in Theorem 2.1.

$\bullet$ \emph{Aperiodicity is still needed.} Recurrent + irreducible alone is not enough --- a periodic chain (e.g.\ alternating between two states) doesn't converge to a stationary marginal; it oscillates. Theorem 2.1 adds aperiodicity to rule this out.

nodes.title: tuning alfa in SES
nodes.content:
In SES: 
$\bullet$ if $\alpha \approx 1$: $\hat{y}_{t+1\mid t} \approx y_t$ (follows the data)

$\bullet$ if $\alpha \approx 0$: $\hat{y}_{t+1\mid t} \approx$ constant

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Choosing $\alpha$ — grid search.}} Try a grid $\alpha \in \{0.01, 0.02, \dots, 0.99\}$. For each $\alpha$, compute the one-step-ahead forecasts on held-out data and evaluate one of:

\textbf{MAE} (Mean Absolute Error):\[ \mathrm{MAE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \left| y_t - \hat{y}_t \right| \]

\textbf{MSE} (Mean Squared Error):\[ \mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \left( y_t - \hat{y}_t \right)^2 \]

\textbf{MAPE} (Mean Absolute Percentage Error):\[ \mathrm{MAPE} = \frac{100\%}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \left| \frac{y_t - \hat{y}_t}{y_t} \right| \]

Pick $\hat\alpha = \arg\min_\alpha \mathrm{(MAE\, /\, MSE\, /\, MAPE)}$. MAE is robust to outliers, MSE penalises large errors more heavily, MAPE is scale-free but blows up when $y_t \approx 0$.

nodes.title: Time series as stochastic processes
nodes.content:
Naive: the \textcolor{red}{TIME SERIES} is a sequence of obs taken over time (see fig) \[ y_{1:T} = (y_1, \dots, y_T) \]
\begin{keydef}
\textbf{Time series as a stochastic process.} A time series is a \textbf{stochastic process} $(Y_t)_{t \ge 0}$: a sequence of random vectors (a multidimensional random variable) indexed by $t$.
\end{keydef} 

Notes:
- Each observed value is a specific realization of the process.
-  that this is not a random variable, nor a random vector. It is a sequence of random variables (or random vectors if multivariate)! So eg the p. of a repeated game.

nodes.title: Example 2. White noise
Markov Property
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MARKOV PROPERTY}}

\begin{keydef}
\textbf{Markov property.} A discrete-time stochastic process $(Y_t)_{t \ge 0}$ with $Y_t \in \mathcal{Y}$ is a \textbf{Markov process} if

$\bullet$ $Y_0 \sim p_0(\cdot)$ \;(initial distribution), and

$\bullet$ for every $t \ge 1$, $Y_t$ depends on the past observations only through $Y_{t-1}$:
\[ p(y_t \mid y_0, y_1, \dots, y_{t-1}) = p(y_t \mid y_{t-1}). \] These are called transition probabilities, and you group them in the transition matrix. 
Note the set $\mathcal{Y}$ of possible values of $Y_t$ is called the \textbf{state space} of the Markov chain.
\end{keydef}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Conditional independence statement.}} The Markov property is equivalent to saying that, for every $t \ge 1$, \[ Y_t \;\perp\!\!\!\perp\; (Y_0, Y_1, \dots, Y_{t-2}) \;\big|\; Y_{t-1}, \]i.e.\ given the immediate past $Y_{t-1}$, the current value $Y_t$ is conditionally independent of everything earlier.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{DAG view.}} A Markov chain is naturally drawn as a directed acyclic graph (DAG):\[ Y_0 \to Y_1 \to Y_2 \to \dots \to Y_{t-1} \to Y_t \to \dots \]\emph{Reading the DAG:} if you remove the node $Y_{t-1}$, the node $Y_t$ becomes disconnected from $(Y_0, \dots, Y_{t-2})$. Graphically, $Y_{t-1}$ d-separates $Y_t$ from its earlier ancestors — exactly the conditional-independence statement above.




**Specifying the Probability law of a markov process**

So the law of the process is fully specified by

$\bullet$ the \textbf{initial distribution} $p_0(\cdot)$ of $Y_0$;

$\bullet$ the family of \textbf{one-step transition kernels} $\{p(y_t \mid y_{t-1}) : t \ge 1\}$.


\textbf{Joint density.} Plugging the Markov property into the general chain rule collapses the joint to one-step transitions only:

$\bullet$ \emph{Non-homogeneous case} (transition kernel varies with $t$):
\[ p_n(y_0, y_1, \dots, y_n) \;=\; p_0(y_0) \prod_{t=1}^{n} p_t(y_t \mid y_{t-1}). \]
$\bullet$ \emph{Homogeneous case} (one common transition kernel $p(\cdot \mid \cdot)$ for every $t$):
\[ p_n(y_0, y_1, \dots, y_n) \;=\; p_0(y_0) \prod_{t=1}^{n} p(y_t \mid y_{t-1}). \]

In both cases the conditional only depends on $y_{t-1}$ (that is the Markov property); the homogeneous case additionally assumes the conditional's \emph{form} does not change with $t$ --- one fixed kernel (or, in the finite-state case, one fixed transition matrix $\mathbf{P}$). The non-homogeneous case allows a different $p_t$ at every time step (or a time-indexed matrix $\mathbf{P}^{(t)}$). 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{TRANSITION MATRIX}}

Finite state space $\mathcal{Y} = \{1, 2, \dots, N\}$. The transition probabilities at time $t$ are\[ p^{(t)}_{i,j} = P(Y_t = j \mid Y_{t-1} = i), \qquad i, j \in \mathcal{Y}. \]Arrange them in a matrix $\mathbf{P}^{(t)}$ with \emph{rows} indexed by the state at $t-1$ and \emph{columns} indexed by the state at $t$:

\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
$t - 1 \;\backslash\; t$ & $1$ & $2$ & $\cdots$ & $N$ \\
\hline
$1$ & $p^{(t)}_{1,1}$ & $p^{(t)}_{1,2}$ & $\cdots$ & $p^{(t)}_{1,N}$ \\
$2$ & $p^{(t)}_{2,1}$ & $p^{(t)}_{2,2}$ & $\cdots$ & $p^{(t)}_{2,N}$ \\
$\vdots$ & $\vdots$ & $\vdots$ & $\ddots$ & $\vdots$ \\
$N$ & $p^{(t)}_{N,1}$ & $p^{(t)}_{N,2}$ & $\cdots$ & $p^{(t)}_{N,N}$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}

\textbf{Row-stochastic:} each row sums to 1, $\sum_{j=1}^{N} p^{(t)}_{i,j} = 1$ for every $i$ and every $t$ — given that you are in state $i$ at $t-1$, you must end up \emph{somewhere} at time $t$.

\textbf{Homogeneous case.} If the transition probabilities do not depend on $t$, i.e.\ $p^{(t)}_{i,j} = p_{i,j}$ for every $t$, then the chain is \textbf{homogeneous}. The superscript drops:\[ \mathbf{P}^{(t)} \equiv \mathbf{P} = \big(p_{i,j}\big)_{i,j \in \mathcal{Y}}, \]a single $N \times N$ matrix that — together with the initial distribution $p_0(\cdot)$ — fully specifies the law of the chain.


Note that and independently distributed time series (Bernoulli example) is automatically markov!

nodes.title: Inference (here the markov chain is observed)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{INFERENCE FOR MARKOV CHAINS}} \emph{(panel of i.i.d.\ chains)}

\textbf{Setting.} When a Markov chain is used as a statistical model, the transition probabilities $p_{i,j}$ are unknown and must be estimated from data. 

Causality: see if transition probabilities chnage after treatment 
Prediction: infer the transition probabilities to predict future values. 

Two data designs:

$\bullet$ \emph{Single long path:} we observe one trajectory $(Y_0, Y_1, \dots, Y_T)$ for $T$ large; estimate $p_{i,j}$ from time averages.

$\bullet$ \emph{Panel:} we observe $n$ short trajectories $(Y_{k,0}, \dots, Y_{k,T})$, $k = 1, \dots, n$, one per individual. This is the Anderson \& Goodman (1957) setting; we focus on this case. In other words, we have a random sample of markov chains characterized by the same transition matrices! 

\textbf{Modelling assumptions.}

\textbf{(M1)} Each individual time series $(Y_{k,t})_{t \ge 0}$ is a \emph{homogeneous} Markov chain with transition matrix $\mathbf{P}$. Recall no statistical mdoel is true... the point is if the model is "reasonable". 

\textbf{(M2)} The $n$ trajectories are i.i.d.\ across individuals: $(Y_{k,t})_{t \ge 0} \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}$ Markov chain with transition matrix $\mathbf{P}$, $k = 1, \dots, n$. So independente: No spillovers + Identical distribution (the marginals are all the same, notice this is different from saying the marginals are time invariant (homogeneous)) = no individaul effects here. 

\textit{Caveats one may want to relax:} higher-order Markov (memory $r > 1$); non-homogeneity ($\mathbf{P}_t$ depends on $t$); individual-specific transition matrices (heterogeneity).

Think about this. Causal inferenc ehere: take 30 ppl inthe control group, 30 in the treatment group, estimate if they have post treatment different transition probabilities. 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Example panel.}} Voter intention data of Example 2: $n = 8$ individuals interviewed monthly at $t = 0, 1, \dots, T = 5$. States: $1 = $ Republican, $2 = $ Democrat, $3 = $ Don't know.

nodes.title: Proof: the counts ratio is the MLE
nodes.content:
Proof: The counts ratio is the MLE



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Proof — the counts ratio is the MLE.}}

\emph{Step 1: define the likelihood.} The \textbf{likelihood} is the probability of observing the data we actually saw, written as a function of the unknown parameter. Here the parameter is the transition matrix $\theta = \mathbf{P} = (p_{i,j})$:\[ L(\mathbf{P};\, \text{data}) \;=\; \mathbb{P}\bigl(\text{data} \,\big|\, \mathbf{P}\bigr), \qquad \text{viewed as a function of } \mathbf{P}. \]

\emph{Step 2: factorise.} Condition on the fixed initial values $y_{k,0}$. Using (M2) i.i.d.\ trajectories, (M1) Markov property + chain rule, and homogeneity (so each one-step conditional is $p_{y_{k,t-1},\, y_{k,t}}$):\[ L(\mathbf{P};\, \underbrace{y_1, \dots, y_n)}_{\text{data from N indiv. eacn observed T times}} \;=\; \underbrace{\prod_{k=1}^{n}\,}_{\text{k individuals}} \underbrace{p_{y_{k,0}, y_{k,1}}\,}_{\text{whatever state the individaul visits}} p_{y_{k,1}, y_{k,2}} \cdots p_{y_{k,T-1}, y_{k,T}}. \]

\emph{Step 3: regroup by transition counts.} The same factor $p_{i,j}$ appears in the product once per observed transition $i \to j$ in the panel (obivously, just grouping probabilities!):\[ L(\mathbf{P};\, \text{data}) \;=\; \prod_{i=1}^{M}\prod_{j=1}^{M} \underbrace{p_{i,j}^{\, n_{i,j}}}_{g(T(x), \theta))}. \] So the statistic $T(x) = \{n_{i,j}\}$ is \textbf{jointly sufficient} for $\mathbf{P}$ 

\emph{Step 4: find MLE by maximise L wrt $p_{i,j}$ and you get: \[ \boxed{\hat p_{i,j} \;=\; \frac{n_{i,j}}{n_{i,+}}, \qquad i, j = 1, \dots, M.} \]

nodes.title: Asymptotics
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{4.2 Asymptotic distributions.}}


Preamble: 

- Experiment, run 1 time, yes no: bernoulli -> run 10 times: binomial  --> CLT -> univariate gaussian (yes,no)
- Experiment, run 1 tine, many possible outcomes k: categorical (ni1, ni2..niM) -> run 10 times (10 individuals): multinomial ---> multivariate gaussian (k outcomes, you see a gaussian k dimensional cloud)

Please notice that multinomial is just repeated bernoulli but with k states!

\textit{Setup for the Markov chain.} Let $\eta_h$ be the initial probability of state $h$ and $n_h(0)$ the number of individuals in state $h$ at $t = 0$. We study the behaviour of $\hat p_{i,j}$ as $n \to \infty$ under the assumption\[ \frac{n_h(0)}{n} \;\longrightarrow\; \eta_h, \qquad h = 1, \dots, M. \]Recall that the MLE of the $i$-th row of $\mathbf{P}$ is $(\hat p_{i,1}, \dots, \hat p_{i,M})$ with $\hat p_{i,j} = n_{i,j}/n_{i,+}$, and\[ (n_{i,1}, \dots, n_{i,M}) \;\sim\; \mathrm{Multinomial}(n_{i,+};\ p_{i,1}, \dots, p_{i,M}). \]Note: $n_{i,+}$ is itself random, since it depends on how often the panel visits state $i$.

$\hat p_{ij}$ is just a ratio, by CLT is multivariate gaussian. It says: average of many independent identically-distributed things is approximately Gaussian, with mean = true mean of one draw, variance = (variance of one draw)/(number of draws).


\textit{Step 1 --- handle the randomness of $n_{i,+}$.} Define\[ \varphi_i \;=\; \sum_{h=1}^{M} \eta_h \sum_{t=1}^{T} p^{(t-1)}_{h,\, i}, \]where $p^{(t-1)}_{h, i}$ is the probability of state $i$ at time $t-1$ given state $h$ at time $0$. So $n\, \varphi_i$ is the expected total number of observations in state $i$ over $t = 0, 1, \dots, T-1$, averaged over the initial distribution. Then\[ \frac{n_{i,+}}{n} \;\longrightarrow\; \varphi_i  \text{as } n \to \infty, \qquad \text{so } n_{i,+} \approx n\, \varphi_i. \]

\textit{Step 2}. Conditional on $n_{i,+}$ known, standard multinomial-MLE theory gives, for $j, h = 1, \dots, M$, $j \neq h$,\[ \mathbb{E}(\hat p_{i,j}) = p_{i,j}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\hat p_{i,j}) = \frac{p_{i,j}(1 - p_{i,j})}{n_{i,+}}, \qquad \mathrm{Cov}(\hat p_{i,j},\ \hat p_{i,h}) = -\frac{p_{i,j}\, p_{i,h}}{n_{i,+}}, \]and an asymptotic multivariate Gaussian distribution for $(\hat p_{i,1}, \dots, \hat p_{i,M})$.


\textit{Result.} The rows of $\hat{\mathbf{P}}$ are \textbf{asymptotically independent} (each multinomial, the joint stays multinomial), and the $i$-th row is approximately multivariate Gaussian:\[ (\hat p_{i,1}, \dots, \hat p_{i,M})^\top \;\approx\; \mathcal{N}_M\bigl(p_i,\ \Sigma_i\bigr), \]
\textit{Approximated variances (plug-in).} The unknowns $p_{i,j}$ and $\varphi_i$ are replaced by consistent estimators: $\hat p_{i,j}$ for $p_{i,j}$, and (using $n_{i,+} \approx n\,\varphi_i$) just the observed row total $n_{i,+}$ in the denominator. This gives the practical estimator\[ \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat p_{i,j}) \;=\; \frac{\hat p_{i,j}\,(1 - \hat p_{i,j})}{n_{i,+}}, \qquad \widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(\hat p_{i,j},\, \hat p_{i,h}) \;=\; -\frac{\hat p_{i,j}\,\hat p_{i,h}}{n_{i,+}} (j \neq h). \]

\textit{Asymptotic confidence intervals.} A level-$(1-\alpha)$ CI for $p_{i,j}$ is\[ \boxed{\;\hat p_{i,j} \;\pm\; z_{\alpha/2}\,\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_{i,j}\,(1 - \hat p_{i,j})}{n_{i,+}}}\;} \]with $z_{\alpha/2}$ the $(1-\alpha/2)$-quantile of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ (e.g.\ $z_{0.025} \approx 1.96$ for $95\%$).

nodes.title: Hidden Markov  Models
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{HIDDEN MARKOV MODELS (HMM)}}

\begin{keydef}
\textbf{Hidden Markov Model (HMM).} An HMM is a discrete-time pair of stochastic processes
\[ \bigl(\, \underbrace{Y_t}_{\text{observation}},\; \underbrace{S_t}_{\text{latent}} \,\bigr)_{t \ge 1}, \quad \text{starting at } S_0, \]
where the distribution that generates the observation $Y_t$ depends on the state of an underlying \emph{unobserved} state process $(S_t)$, such that:

$\bullet$ \textbf{(1) Latent homogeneous Markov state process.} $(S_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is a homogeneous Markov chain on a finite state space $\mathcal{S} = \{1, \dots, M\}$ with initial distribution $\pi$ and transition matrix $\mathbf{P} = (p_{i,j})$, $p_{i,j} = P(S_t = j \mid S_{t-1} = i)$.

$\bullet$ \textbf{(2) Conditional independence of the observations.} Given the latent path $(S_t)_{t \ge 0}$, the $Y_t$'s are conditionally independent and each $Y_t$ depends only on $S_t$.

\textbf{Equivalently,} the law of an HMM is fully specified by:
\[ S_0 \;\sim\; \pi, \qquad S_t \mid S_{t-1} = i \;\sim\; \text{Categorical}(p_{i,1}, \dots, p_{i,M}), \qquad Y_t \mid S_t = j \;\sim\; p(y_t \mid \theta_j^*), \]
i.e.\ an initial distribution on the states, a discrete transition matrix for the hidden chain, and an emission distribution per state (parameters $\{\theta_j^*\}_{j=1}^M$).
\end{keydef}

\emph{When is it useful?} ARMA-type models assume stationarity. HMMs are tailored for \emph{non-stationary} series with change points / regime switches — e.g.\ speech recognition, business-cycle detection, unbounded-count series (Poisson observation "number of calls in one hour"  ) where the rate switches between states. Why not modelign it with a poisson? becasse poisson is st mean and variance coincide (do not want this constraint)

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Toy 3-regime Gaussian HMM.}} A simple example with three regimes is\[ Y_t = \begin{cases} \mu_1 + e_t & \text{if } S_t = 1, \\ \mu_2 + e_t & \text{if } S_t = 2, \\ \mu_3 + e_t & \text{if } S_t = 3, \end{cases} \qquad e_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2). \]More compactly, $Y_t = \mu_{S_t} + e_t$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The "equation" of the hidden chain (3-regime example).}} For this toy example, $K = 3$ and the state space is $\mathcal{S} = \{1, 2, 3\}$. The conditional law of $S_t$ given $S_{t-1} = i$ is the categorical distribution given by row $i$ of $\mathbf{P}$:
\[ S_t \mid S_{t-1} = i \;\sim\; \text{Categorical}\bigl(p_{i,1},\, p_{i,2},\, p_{i,3}\bigr), \]
i.e.\ $P(S_t = j \mid S_{t-1} = i) = p_{i,j}$, plus the initial law $S_0 \sim \pi = (\pi_1, \pi_2, \pi_3)$. This is the "equation" of the hidden Markov chain --- once you draw $S_t$ from this categorical, the observation is $Y_t = \mu_{S_t} + e_t$.

\textit{Note:} the observed process $(Y_t)$ itself is generally \emph{not} Markov — observing $Y_{t-1}$ does not pin down $S_{t-1}$. The Markov property lives at the level of the \emph{hidden} chain.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Specifying the law of an HMM.}} It follows that the probability law of the hidden Markov process $\bigl((S_t, Y_t)\bigr)_{t \ge 0}$ is specified by assigning:

$\bullet$ the \textbf{initial distribution} of the hidden state: $S_0 \sim \pi$ on $\mathcal{S} = \{1, \dots, M\}$, that is $(p_0(1), ... , p_0(k))$; 

$\bullet$ the \textbf{transition matrix} of the hidden chain: $A = \mathbf{P} = (p_{i,j})_{i,j \in \mathcal{S}}$ with $p_{i,j} = P(S_t = j \mid S_{t-1} = i)$;

$\bullet$ the \textbf{emission distributions} $\{p(y \mid s) : s \in \mathcal{S}\}$, one per state

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{DAG view of an HMM — reading conditional independence.}}

nodes.title: Example emission matrices
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE EMISSION MATRICES}}

Recall the emission distributions are the probability distribution of the observable variable $Y_t$ given the state $S_t = j$, for $j = 1, \dots, K$. Two standard cases.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. Discrete (non-parametric) case.}} Suppose $Y_t$ takes values in the finite set $\{1, \dots, M\}$. The general (non-parametric) form of the emission distribution in state $j$ is

\[ Y_t \mid S_t = j \;\sim\; \bigl(\, \underbrace{P(Y_t = 1 \mid S_t = j)}_{b_{j,1}}, \;\dots,\; \underbrace{P(Y_t = i \mid S_t = j)}_{b_{j,i}}, \;\dots,\; \underbrace{P(Y_t = M \mid S_t = j)}_{b_{j,M}} \,\bigr), \]

i.e.\ we let $P(Y_t = y \mid S_t = j) \equiv b_{j,y}$, $y = 1, \dots, M$. Collecting the emission probabilities $b_{j,y}$ in the \emph{emission matrix}

\[ B = [b_{j,y}]_{j=1,\dots,K;\; y=1,\dots,M}, \]

we use the compact notation $\phi = (A, B, \pi)$ to represent the HMM. Specification of the HMM then requires choosing the number of states $K$ and the probability matrices $A$, $B$ and the initial vector $\pi$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. Parametric case --- Poisson emissions.}} In other cases one may want a parametric emission distribution, so that $Y_t \mid S_t = j \sim p(\,\cdot \mid \theta_j^*)$, $j = 1, \dots, K$. For example, for the earthquakes data (unbounded counts), one could assume
\[ Y_t \mid (S_t = j) \;\sim\; \text{Poisson}(\theta_j^*), \]
that is, at state $j$, $Y_t$ has a Poisson distribution with parameter $\theta_j^*$. Note how the parameter can switch across states!

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why this fixes the plain-Poisson defects.}} A single Poisson forces (i) mean $=$ variance, (ii) no serial dependence. Letting the rate \emph{switch} with a Markov chain breaks all three:

$\bullet$ \textbf{Different mean and variance per regime.} Within state $j$, both equal $\lambda_j^*$, but across regimes they differ --- a "quiet" state has small mean \emph{and} small variance, an "active" one has large mean \emph{and} large variance.

$\bullet$ \textbf{Autocorrelation.} Sticky regimes ($p_{j,j}$ near $1$) mean neighbouring $Y_t$'s likely share the same rate, so
\[ \text{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t+h}) \;=\; \text{Cov}(\lambda_{S_t}^*, \lambda_{S_{t+h}}^*) \;>\; 0. \]
No additive $\epsilon$ needed --- the dependence comes from persistence of the hidden chain.

nodes.title: Specification
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{1. MODEL SPECIFICATION}}

Choosing the number $K$ of hidden states is a natural first question. In some applications, $K$ is suggested by knowledge of the domain under study. In other cases, one can try a few different values of $K$ and compare the performance of the resulting models.

nodes.title: Estimation
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{2. ESTIMATION OF THE UNKNOWN PARAMETERS}}

We estimate the unknown parameters $\phi = (A, B, \pi)$ of an HMM by \emph{maximum likelihood}. Focus on the \emph{discrete non-parametric case}: $Y_t \in \{1, \dots, M\}$, latent states $S_t \in \{1, \dots, K\}$.

The likelihood is the joint probability of the observed sequence $y_{1:T}$, read as a function of $\phi$.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 1 --- Marginalise the hidden path.}} Since $S_{0:T}$ takes \emph{some} path in every realisation, the events $\{S_{0:T} = s_{0:T}\}$ partition the sample space. By the law of total probability:
\[ L(\phi \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; P(Y_{1:T} = y_{1:T} \mid \phi) \;\underbrace{=}_{\text{a sum over all possible b}}\; \sum_{s_{0:T} \,\in\, \{1, \dots, K\}^{T+1}} P(Y_{1:T} = y_{1:T},\, S_{0:T} = s_{0:T} \mid \phi) \underbrace{=}_{\text{chain rule}} \underbrace{P(Y_{1:T} \mid S_{0:T},\, \phi)}_{(\mathrm{A})\,\text{ obs.\ given path}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{P(S_{0:T} \mid \phi)}_{(\mathrm{B})\,\text{ path probability}}. \]

Explaining notation: The sum is over all $K^{T+1}$ possible state paths $(s_0, s_1, \dots, s_T)$. So we have T+1 terms, each can take K values. 


\emph{A direct evaluation of such joint probability may be involved, because the temporal dependence of the process $(Y_t)$ may be complex. Fortunately, after extracting latents, we can exploit the conditional independence structure of the HMM.} We derive it step by step.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 3 --- Compute $(\mathrm{A})$ via conditional independence of observations.}} Chain rule then HMM emission assumption (each $Y_t$ depends only on its own $S_t$ given the path):
\[ (\mathrm{A}) \;=\; \prod_{t=1}^{T} P(Y_t = y_t \mid S_t = s_t,\, \phi) \;=\; \prod_{t=1}^{T} b_{s_t, y_t}. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 4 --- Compute $(\mathrm{B})$ via Markov property of the chain.}} Chain rule then Markov assumption (each $S_t$ depends only on $S_{t-1}$):
\[ (\mathrm{B}) \;=\; P(S_0 \mid \phi) \prod_{t=1}^{T} P(S_t \mid S_{t-1},\, \phi) \;=\; \pi_{s_0} \prod_{t=1}^{T} p_{s_{t-1}, s_t}. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Step 5 --- Combine.}} Multiply $(\mathrm{A})$ and $(\mathrm{B})$ inside the sum:
\[ \boxed{\; L(\phi \mid y_{1:T}) \;=\; \sum_{s_{0:T} \,\in\, \{1, \dots, K\}^{T+1}} \underbrace{\pi_{s_0}}_{\text{initial}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\prod_{t=1}^{T} p_{s_{t-1}, s_t}}_{\text{transitions}} \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\prod_{t=1}^{T} b_{s_t, y_t}}_{\text{emissions}}  \;=\; \sum_{s_{0:T}} \pi_{s_0}\, p_{s_0, s_1}\, b_{s_1, y_1}\, p_{s_1, s_2}\, b_{s_2, y_2}\, \cdots\, p_{s_{T-1}, s_T}\, b_{s_T, y_T}. \qquad (2) \;} \]


\emph{Exercise.} Write the expression of the likelihood in the discrete parametric case, assuming that the emission distribution is Poisson.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Maximisation.}} The MLE is $\hat\phi = \arg\max_{\phi} L(\phi \mid y_{1:T})$. Direct numerical maximisation is feasible but expensive; in practice, the EM algorithm (\emph{Baum-Welch} for HMMs) is the standard iterative procedure.

nodes.title: Decoding
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{3. DECODING}}

Estimate the latent state sequence $s_{1:T}$ given observed $y_{1:T}$ (treat $s_0$ as fixed, and $\phi$ as known or replaced by its MLE).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Local criterion.}} For each $t = 1, \dots, T$, pick the marginally most likely state:
\[ s_t^* \;=\; \arg\max_s \gamma_t(s), \qquad \gamma_t(s) \;\equiv\; P(S_t = s \mid y_{1:T}, \phi). \]
\emph{Issue.} The resulting sequence $s_{1:T}^*$ may include zero-probability transitions ($p_{i,j} = 0$), making the global path infeasible.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Global criterion --- Viterbi.}} Find the path that maximises the joint conditional probability:
\[ \max_{s_{0:T}} P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T \mid Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T, \phi). \]
Given the data, and the parameters, what is the most likely hidden state? 

This conditional probability can be computed using Bayes theorem. However, we can more easily exploit the computations already carried out for the MLE. Notice that
\[ \begin{aligned} & P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T,\, Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi) \\ & \underbrace{=}_{\text{chain rule}} P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T \mid Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T, \phi)\, P(Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi), \end{aligned} \]
where the latter factor on the right-hand side does not depend on $s_{0:T}$. Therefore, maximising the conditional joint probability with respect to $s_{0:T}$ is equivalent to maximising the joint probability $P(S_0 = s_0, \dots, S_T = s_T,\, Y_1 = y_1, \dots, Y_T = y_T \mid \phi)$ wrt phi. Now we need to optimize the same thing by $S_{0:T}$

nodes.title: Example — Nile river
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE --- Nile river data}}

In LAB 2 we consider a few examples on the use of HMMs with R, using the R package \texttt{depmixS4}.

The following example considers the \emph{Nile river data}, available in R, which provides the measurements of the annual flow of the Nile river in the period 1871--1970. We envisage a change point around the year 1898, when the construction of the first dam in Aswan was started. This suggests to fit an HMM with $K = 2$ states --- so $(S_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is a Markov chain with state space $\mathcal{S} = \{1, 2\}$ --- and to assume a \emph{Gaussian emission distribution} with state-specific parameters:
\[ \begin{aligned} Y_t \mid S_t = 1 &\;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\mu_1^*, \sigma_1^*), \\ Y_t \mid S_t = 2 &\;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\mu_2^*, \sigma_2^*), \end{aligned} \]
where the (unknown) parameters are $\theta_1^* = (\mu_1^*, \sigma_1^*)$ and $\theta_2^* = (\mu_2^*, \sigma_2^*)$. We also fix the initial distribution as
\[ \pi \;=\; \bigl(\, \pi_1 = 0, \;\; \pi_2 = 1 \,\bigr). \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The "equation" of the hidden chain.}} For this 2-state chain, the conditional law of $S_t$ given $S_{t-1} = i$ is the categorical distribution given by row $i$ of $\mathbf{P}$:
\[ S_t \mid S_{t-1} = i \;\sim\; \text{Categorical}\bigl(p_{i,1}, p_{i,2}, \dots, p_{i,K}\bigr), \]
i.e.\ $P(S_t = j \mid S_{t-1} = i) = p_{i,j}$, plus the initial law $S_0 \sim \pi$. This is the "equation" of a Markov chain.





\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MLE of the transition matrix.}} The maximum likelihood estimates of the transition matrix, provided by \texttt{depmixS4}, are
\begin{tabular}{c|cc} $t-1 \backslash t$ & $1$ & $2$ \\ \hline $1$ & $1.00$ & $0.00$ \\ $2$ & $0.04$ & $0.97$ \end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MLE of the emission parameters.}} The MLEs of the parameters $\theta_j^*$ are
\[ \hat\theta_1^* = (\hat\mu_1^*, \hat\sigma_1^*) = (850.57,\; 124.45), \qquad \hat\theta_2^* = (\hat\mu_2^*, \hat\sigma_2^*) = (1097.15,\; 133.75). \]

\emph{Remark.} Reporting the MLEs is not enough. One should also provide the \textbf{standard errors} of the MLEs (possibly approximated by bootstrap techniques), or at least their \emph{asymptotic} standard errors, obtained from the asymptotic properties of MLEs. The computation of the standard errors for the MLEs of the fitted HMM, using the R package \texttt{depmixS4}, is illustrated in Lab 2.

nodes.title: Exercise — weather/activity filtering (state is unobserved)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXERCISE --- Filtering: weather $\to$ activity}}

\textbf{Setup.} A person's daily activity depends on the weather, which is hidden. We observe only the activity.

$\bullet$ Hidden $\mathcal{S} = \{1 = \text{sunny},\, 2 = \text{rainy}\}$ ($K = 2$), observed $\mathcal{Y} = \{1 = \text{walk},\, 2 = \text{shop},\, 3 = \text{clean}\}$ ($M = 3$).

$\bullet$ Initial $\pi = (P(S_1 = \text{sunny}), P(S_1 = \text{rainy})) = (0.6,\, 0.4)$.

\textbf{Transition matrix} $A$ (rows = state at $t-1$, columns = state at $t$):
\begin{tabular}{c|cc} $t-1 \backslash t$ & sunny & rainy \\ \hline sunny & $0.7$ & $0.3$ \\ rainy & $0.4$ & $0.6$ \end{tabular}

\textbf{Emission matrix} $B$ (rows = state, columns = activity):
\begin{tabular}{c|ccc} $S_t \backslash Y_t$ & walk & shop & clean \\ \hline sunny & $0.6$ & $0.3$ & $0.1$ \\ rainy & $0.1$ & $0.4$ & $0.5$ \end{tabular}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The universal recipe (forward algorithm).}} Define
\[ \alpha_t(j) \;:=\; P(S_t = j,\; y_{1:t}) \quad\text{(joint "score": data observed so far AND being in state $j$ now)}. \]
One rule for every step:
\[ \boxed{\; \alpha_t(j) \;=\; \underbrace{b_{j, y_t}}_{\text{today's evidence}} \cdot \underbrace{\sum_{i} \alpha_{t-1}(i)\, p_{i,j}}_{\text{yesterday's belief, pushed forward through } A}, \qquad \alpha_1(j) \;=\; \pi_j\, b_{j, y_1}. \;} \]
\emph{In words:} transition the old belief through $A$, then weight by today's emission. Past observations are never thrown away --- they live inside $\alpha_{t-1}$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(a) After $y_1 = \text{walk}$.}} No transition needed yet (start of chain):
\[ \alpha_1(\text{sunny}) = \pi_{\text{sunny}}\, b_{\text{sunny, walk}} = 0.6 \cdot 0.6 = 0.36, \qquad \alpha_1(\text{rainy}) = 0.4 \cdot 0.1 = 0.04. \]
Walking is far more compatible with sunny ($0.6$ vs $0.1$) $\Rightarrow$ score ratio $9{:}1$ in favour of sunny.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{(b) After $y_2 = \text{shop}$.}}

\emph{Predict $S_2$ from history:} push $\alpha_1$ through $A$:
\[ \text{pred}_2(\text{sunny}) = 0.36 \cdot 0.7 + 0.04 \cdot 0.4 = 0.268, \qquad \text{pred}_2(\text{rainy}) = 0.36 \cdot 0.3 + 0.04 \cdot 0.6 = 0.132. \]
\emph{Weight by today's emission:}
\[ \alpha_2(\text{sunny}) = 0.268 \cdot 0.3 = 0.0804, \qquad \alpha_2(\text{rainy}) = 0.132 \cdot 0.4 = 0.0528. \]
Shopping is mildly more compatible with rainy ($0.4$ vs $0.3$), pulling the belief from $9{:}1$ down to roughly $1.5{:}1$; sunny stays ahead because the chain is sticky ($p_{\text{sunny}, \text{sunny}} = 0.7$).

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Take-aways.}}

$\bullet$ Two-step recipe at every $t$: (1) push the old belief through $A$ to get the predicted prior; (2) multiply by the emission to fold in today's evidence.

$\bullet$ $\alpha_t(j) = P(S_t = j, y_{1:t})$ is a \emph{joint}, not a posterior. Their relative magnitudes already tell you which state is more likely; summing them gives the data likelihood $P(y_{1:t}) = \sum_j \alpha_t(j)$ for free.

$\bullet$ This is exactly the \emph{forward algorithm} --- the engine inside HMM likelihood evaluation, filtering, and (with a small modification: $\max$ instead of $\sum$) Viterbi decoding.

nodes.title: State space models (SSM)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{STATE SPACE MODELS (SSM)}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{One-line intuition.}}  A latent process $(\theta_t)$ evolves Markovianly in its state space, and each observation $Y_t$ is drawn from a distribution determined only by the current state.

So the time series you see is the output of a dynamic system  (the latent procss) + some random disturbances. What is nice is that the underlying dynamic system can have a trends, seasonal componetns, regressive components etc so there is a lot of flesibilty. On top of this they have a very nice probabilityic structure (embed in everything you are doing). 




\begin{keydef}
\textbf{State-space model (SSM).} An SSM is a discrete-time pair of stochastic processes
\[ \bigl(\, \underbrace{Y_t}_{\text{observation}},\; \underbrace{\theta_t}_{\text{latent}} \,\bigr)_{t \ge 1}, \quad \text{starting at } \theta_0, \]
where the distribution that generates the observation $Y_t$ depends on the state of an underlying \emph{unobserved} state process $(\theta_t)$, such that:

$\bullet$ \textbf{(1) Latent Markov state process.} $(\theta_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is a Markov process with continuous state space $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p$, initial distribution $\pi$ and transition kernel $f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})$. (In HMMs the state space is discrete $\mathcal{S} = \{1, \dots, M\}$ and the kernel is a matrix; here $\Theta$ is continuous.)

$\bullet$ \textbf{(2) Conditional independence of the observations.} Given the latent path $(\theta_t)_{t \ge 0}$, the $Y_t$'s are conditionally independent and each $Y_t$ depends only on $\theta_t$.

\textbf{Equivalently,} the law of an SSM is fully specified by:
\[ \theta_0 \;\sim\; \pi, \qquad \theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1} \;\sim\; f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1}), \qquad Y_t \mid \theta_t \;\sim\; f(y_t \mid \theta_t), \]
i.e.\ an initial law on the state, a transition kernel for the state, and an emission kernel for the observation.
\end{keydef}



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Two layers of inference: don't confuse them.}}

The transition kernel $f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})$ plays \emph{two different roles}, depending on which question you are asking.

$\bullet$ \textbf{(A) Model ingredient (input).} When the model is fully known, $f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1})$ is \emph{given}. You use it \emph{inside} the algorithms (it's the engine of the recursive Bayes update: "carry yesterday's belief forward through the transition"), but it is not the \emph{target} of inference. The four canonical inference tasks --- filtering, smoothing, prediction, decoding --- all assume the model is known and use the transition kernel as an ingredient.

$\bullet$ \textbf{(B) Unknown parameter (target).} When the model has unknown parameters $\phi$, the transition becomes $f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1}; \phi)$ and you genuinely want to learn it from data. In HMMs, $\phi$ contains the entire matrix $\mathbf{P} = (p_{i,j})$. This is a \emph{separate} inference question:

- \emph{Observed Markov chain:} count transitions, $\hat p_{i,j} = n_{i,j} / n_{i,+}$ (the panel-survey exercises).
- \emph{Hidden Markov chain (HMM):} the chain is unobserved, so counting is not possible. Use MLE. \emph{Workflow.} Parameter inference first ($\hat\phi$ from the data), then plug $\hat\phi$ in and do state inference. The four canonical tasks live in the second layer; the transition kernel is itself a \emph{target} only when you're in the first layer.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Specialisations / next topics.}}

$\bullet$ The four canonical inference tasks --- \emph{filtering} $f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:t})$, \emph{smoothing} $f(\theta_t \mid y_{1:T})$ , \emph{prediction} $f(\theta_{t+h}, Y_{t+h} \mid y_{1:t})$ --- all use only the joint factorisation above. The Kalman filter, forward algorithm, Viterbi and particle filter are just \emph{efficient ways to do the recursive Bayes update} on that joint.

Note Smoothing for HMM: applies the "local" criterion. For HMM we used viterbi, the global criterion (so smoothign is more or less decoding).

nodes.title: Example SSMs
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLES OF SSMs --- each process in two forms: directly observed (A) and SSM-lifted (B)}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Canonical DLM template.}} Every Part (B) below is a \emph{specialisation} of:
\begin{keydef}
\textbf{General DLM (linear Gaussian SSM).}

\emph{State equation:} $\;\theta_t \;=\; G_t\, \theta_{t-1} \;+\; w_t,\qquad w_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, W_t),\quad \theta_t \in \mathbb{R}^p.$

\emph{Observation equation:} $\;Y_t \;=\; F_t\, \theta_t \;+\; v_t,\qquad v_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\, V_t),\quad Y_t \in \mathbb{R}^q.$

\emph{Independence:} $\{w_t\} \perp \{v_s\}$ and both $\perp\ \theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0, C_0)$.
\end{keydef}
Each example below picks $(G, F, W, V)$ (often time-invariant). Optional additive inputs $u_t$ (constant drift, exogenous regressors) extend the state eq. to $\theta_t = G \theta_{t-1} + u_t + w_t$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Specialisation tree.}}
\[ \underbrace{\text{General SSM}}_{\text{any } f(\theta_t \mid \theta_{t-1}),\, f(y_t \mid \theta_t)} \begin{cases} \xrightarrow[\text{state} = \mathbb{R}^p]{\text{linear Gaussian}} \underbrace{\text{DLM}}_{\text{template above}} & \text{(all examples below)} \\[6pt] \xrightarrow[\text{state} = \{1,\dots,K\}]{\text{discretise state}} \underbrace{\text{HMM}}_{S_t \mid S_{t-1} = i \sim \text{Cat}(p_{i,\cdot}),\; Y_t \mid S_t \sim f(\cdot \mid \theta^*_{S_t})} & \text{(separate snippets)} \end{cases} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 1 --- Simple random walk.}}

\textbf{(A) Directly observed.} A player starts with capital $y_0 > 0$. Each step: gain $+1$ w.p.\ $p$, loss $-1$ w.p.\ $1-p$. With $Z_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} (\pm 1)$:
\[ Y_t \;=\; Y_{t-1} + Z_t \;=\; y_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{t} Z_i. \]
$Z_t$ iid and independent of past $Y$'s $\Rightarrow$ Markov. With $y_0 = 0$, $E[Z_t] = 0$: $E[Y_t] = 0$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = t\sigma^2$ --- variance grows linearly, so the walk is \textbf{non-stationary}. \emph{Continuous-time limit} (small steps in rapid succession): \textbf{Brownian motion}. The recursion works for any iid $Z_t$, not just $\pm 1$.

\textbf{(B) SSM lift --- RW + noise (local-level model).} \emph{Specialise the DLM template:} $G = 1,\; F = 1,\; W = \sigma_z^2,\; V = \sigma_\varepsilon^2$:
\begin{keydef}
\textbf{Random walk + noise (local-level model).}

\emph{State equation (latent):} $\;x_t = x_{t-1} + z_t,\quad z_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_z^2),\quad x_0$ given.

\emph{Observation equation:} $\;y_t = x_t + \varepsilon_t,\quad \varepsilon_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\varepsilon^2),\quad \{\varepsilon_t\} \perp \{z_s\}.$
\end{keydef}

The \emph{signal-to-noise ratio} $\sigma_z^2 / \sigma_\varepsilon^2$ controls how much $y_t$ reveals about $x_t$:

$\bullet$ $\sigma_\varepsilon^2 \to 0$: $y_t = x_t$ --- recover Part (A) (state observed exactly).

$\bullet$ $\sigma_z^2 \to 0$: state frozen at $x_0$, $y_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(x_0, \sigma_\varepsilon^2)$ --- iid noise around a constant.

\emph{Moments (with $x_0 = 0$):} $E[y_t] = 0$, $\mathrm{Var}(y_t) = t\sigma_z^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2$ --- non-stationary.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 2 --- Random walk with drift.}}

\textbf{(A) Directly observed.} Same recursion as Example 1, but now the increments have non-zero mean: $\mu := E[Z_t] \ne 0$ (the \emph{drift}), $\sigma^2 := \mathrm{Var}(Z_t)$. Decompose into trend + zero-mean walk:
\[ Y_t \;=\; \underbrace{(y_0 + t\mu)}_{\text{deterministic trend}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{t} (Z_i - \mu)}_{\text{zero-mean random walk}}. \]
\emph{Non-stationary:} $E[Y_t] = y_0 + t\mu$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = t\sigma^2$.

\textbf{(B) SSM lift --- RW + drift + noise.} \emph{Specialise the DLM template:} $G = 1,\; F = 1,\; W = \sigma_z^2,\; V = \sigma_\varepsilon^2$, plus deterministic input $u_t \equiv \mu$ in the state equation:
\[ x_t = x_{t-1} + \mu + z_t, \qquad y_t = x_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad z_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_z^2),\; \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\varepsilon^2). \]
\emph{Moments:} $E[y_t \mid x_0] = x_0 + t\mu$, $\mathrm{Var}(y_t \mid x_0) = t\sigma_z^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2$. \emph{Limits:} $\sigma_\varepsilon^2 \to 0$ recovers Part (A); $\sigma_z^2 \to 0$ gives the classical \emph{linear-trend regression} $y_t = x_0 + \mu t + \varepsilon_t$.

\emph{Vs.\ local linear trend DLM.} A "DLM with a trend" usually means level + slope both random:
\[ \mu_t = \mu_{t-1} + \beta_{t-1} + w_{1,t}, \quad \beta_t = \beta_{t-1} + w_{2,t}, \quad Y_t = \mu_t + \varepsilon_t. \]
This Part (B) is the degenerate case $W_2 = 0$ --- slope $\beta_t \equiv \mu$ is a deterministic constant, not a random walk.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 3 --- AR(1), continuous-state Markov.}}

\textbf{(A) Directly observed.} Discrete-time Markov process on $\mathbb{R}$:
\[ Y_t \;=\; \varphi\, Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2). \]
Three regimes:

$\bullet$ $\varphi = 1$: \emph{random walk} --- the Gaussian, continuous-state version of Example 1 ($\pm 1 \to \varepsilon_t \in \mathbb{R}$, state space $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$).

$\bullet$ $|\varphi| < 1$: \emph{stationary}, mean-reverting toward $0$, stationary variance $\sigma^2/(1-\varphi^2)$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Proof: $|\varphi| < 1$ $\Rightarrow$ weakly stationary.}} Unroll the recursion from $Y_0$:
\[ Y_t \;=\; \varphi^t Y_0 \;+\; \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \varphi^k\, \varepsilon_{t-k}. \]
We check the three conditions of weak stationarity (assume $\varepsilon_t$ iid with mean $0$, variance $\sigma^2$, and $\varepsilon_t \perp Y_0$).

\emph{1.\ Constant mean.}
\[ E[Y_t] \;=\; \varphi^t\, E[Y_0] \;+\; \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \varphi^k\, \underbrace{E[\varepsilon_{t-k}]}_{=\,0} \;=\; \varphi^t\, E[Y_0]. \]
With $E[Y_0] = 0$ (e.g.\ start from the stationary distribution, meaning p()): $E[Y_t] = 0$ for all $t$. Otherwise $\varphi^t E[Y_0] \to 0$ geometrically (asymptotic mean stationarity). \quad $\checkmark$

\emph{2.\ Constant, finite variance.} By independence of shocks and $Y_0$:
\[ \mathrm{Var}(Y_t) \;=\; \varphi^{2t}\, \mathrm{Var}(Y_0) \;+\; \sigma^2 \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} \varphi^{2k}. \]
The geometric series $\sum_{k\ge 0} \varphi^{2k}$ converges iff $\varphi^2 < 1$, i.e.\ $|\varphi| < 1$, with limit $1/(1-\varphi^2)$. Starting from $\mathrm{Var}(Y_0) = \sigma^2/(1-\varphi^2)$:
\[ \gamma(0) \;:=\; \mathrm{Var}(Y_t) \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2}{1-\varphi^2} \qquad \text{for all } t. \quad \checkmark \]

\emph{3.\ Autocovariance depends only on lag $h$.} For $h \ge 0$, multiply $Y_{t+h} = \varphi Y_{t+h-1} + \varepsilon_{t+h}$ iteratively and use $\varepsilon_{t+j} \perp Y_t$ for $j \ge 1$:
\[ \gamma(h) \;:=\; \mathrm{Cov}(Y_t, Y_{t+h}) \;=\; \mathrm{Cov}\!\left(Y_t,\; \varphi^h Y_t + \sum_{j=1}^{h} \varphi^{h-j} \varepsilon_{t+j}\right) \;=\; \varphi^h\, \gamma(0). \]
No $t$-dependence. \quad $\checkmark$

\emph{Autocorrelation:} $\rho(h) = \gamma(h)/\gamma(0) = \varphi^{|h|}$ --- decays geometrically, sign alternates if $\varphi < 0$.

\emph{Why the other regimes fail.} $|\varphi| = 1$: $\sum \varphi^{2k} = t$, so $\mathrm{Var}(Y_t) = t\sigma^2 \to \infty$. $|\varphi| > 1$: $\varphi^{2t} \to \infty$, variance explodes. In both cases condition (2) fails.

Continuous-state Markov processes are the building block for SSMs.

\textbf{(B) SSM lift --- AR(1) as a degenerate DLM.} \emph{Specialise the DLM template:} $G = \varphi,\; F = 1,\; W = \sigma^2,\; V = 0$, with $\theta_t := Y_t$:
\[ \theta_t = \varphi\, \theta_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad Y_t = \theta_t. \]
The "latent" state isn't really hidden ($V = 0 \Rightarrow Y_t$ reveals it exactly), but it formally satisfies the DLM template. A non-degenerate lift would set $V = \sigma_\nu^2 > 0$ (analogous to Examples 1B and 2B), giving an AR(1) corrupted by measurement noise.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{EXAMPLE 4 --- AR($p$) via state augmentation.}}

\emph{Why a separate example.} AR($p$) remembers $p$ lags, so it is \emph{not} Markov of order $1$ in the scalar $Y_t$ alone --- there's no "directly observed" Part (A) that fits the templates above without a trick. The trick: \textbf{augment the state} so the model becomes Markov-1 in a vector. Then it fits the DLM template (Part B-style) even though we're still observing $Y_t$ exactly.

\emph{Specialise the DLM template:} state $\theta_t \in \mathbb{R}^p$ stacks the last $p$ values,
\[ \theta_t \;:=\; (Y_t,\, Y_{t-1},\, \dots,\, Y_{t-p+1})^\top, \]
$G$ is the \emph{companion matrix}, $W = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma^2, 0, \dots, 0)$, $F = (1, 0, \dots, 0)$, $V = 0$:
\[ G = \begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 & \phi_2 & \cdots & \phi_p \\ 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \ddots & & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad w_t = (\varepsilon_t, 0, \dots, 0)^\top, \qquad F = (1, 0, \dots, 0). \]
Top row of $G$ encodes the AR equation; rows 2 to $p$ form a \emph{shift register} copying each value down one slot. $F$ picks the top component as the observation.

\emph{Worked AR(2)} ($p = 2$). $\theta_t = (Y_t, Y_{t-1})^\top$, $G = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} \phi_1 & \phi_2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, $w_t = (\varepsilon_t, 0)^\top$, $F = (1, 0)$:
\[ G\, \theta_{t-1} + w_t \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 Y_{t-1} + \phi_2 Y_{t-2} + \varepsilon_t \\ Y_{t-1} \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} Y_t \\ Y_{t-1} \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \theta_t. \;\checkmark \qquad F\, \theta_t = Y_t. \;\checkmark \]
\emph{Why keep the second slot if $F$ ignores it?} The next transition needs $Y_{t-1}$ to compute $Y_{t+1} = \phi_1 Y_t + \phi_2 Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_{t+1}$. The bottom slot is a \emph{delay line} holding the memory required by row 1 of $G$ at the next step (top slot $=$ "value emitted now", bottom slot $=$ "value kept for next time").

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Summary table.}}

\begin{tabular}{l|l|l|l|l}
Model & Layers & State $\theta_t$ & Transition & Observation \\
\hline
Ex.\ 1A (simple RW) & 1 (observed) & $Y_t \in \mathbb{Z}$ & $+Z_t \;(\pm 1)$, iid & $Y_t = \theta_t$ \\
Ex.\ 1B (RW + noise) & 2 (DLM, $G=F=1$) & $x_t \in \mathbb{R}$ & $+z_t$ & $y_t = x_t + \varepsilon_t$ \\
Ex.\ 2A (RW + drift) & 1 (observed) & $Y_t \in \mathbb{R}$ & $+\mu + Z_t$ & $Y_t = \theta_t$ \\
Ex.\ 2B (RW + drift + noise) & 2 (DLM, $G=F=1$, drift $\mu$) & $x_t \in \mathbb{R}$ & $+\mu + z_t$ & $y_t = x_t + \varepsilon_t$ \\
Ex.\ 3A (AR(1)) & 1 (observed) & $Y_t \in \mathbb{R}$ & $\varphi Y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$ & $Y_t = \theta_t$ \\
Ex.\ 3B (AR(1) as DLM) & 1 (degen., $V=0$) & $Y_t \in \mathbb{R}$ & $\varphi\, \theta_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$ & $Y_t = \theta_t$ \\
Ex.\ 4 (AR($p$) as DLM) & 1 (degen., $V=0$, state augmented) & $\mathbb{R}^p$ (lags) & companion $G$ & $Y_t = (1, 0, \dots, 0)\, \theta_t$ \\
HMM & 2 & $\{1, \dots, K\}$ & matrix $\mathbf{P}$ & $Y_t \mid S_t = j \sim f(\cdot \mid \theta_j^*)$ \\
\end{tabular}

nodes.title: Bayesian statistics
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{BAYESIAN STATISTICS --- Bayes' rule, derivation and intuition}}

You forecast the next value to be A. But you want to deal with uncertainty... the soltuon is probability

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The goal.}} We want to know
\[ P(A \mid B), \]
i.e.\emph{"after seeing evidence $B$, how likely is hypothesis $A$?"}. 



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{From the definition of conditional probability.}} For two events $A, B$,
\[ P(A \mid B) \;=\; \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}, \qquad P(B \mid A) \;=\; \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)}. \]
Read: "among the worlds where $B$ holds, what fraction also has $A$ ?"

\emph{The problem.} The joint $P(A \cap B)$ is usually hard to compute directly. Bayes' rule is the trick to express it in terms of quantities we can compute.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Derivation in three lines.}} Using:
\[ P(A \cap B) \;=\; P(A \mid B)\, P(B) \qquad \text{and} \qquad P(A \cap B) \;=\; P(B \mid A)\, P(A). \]
you get
\[ \boxed{\; P(A \mid B) \;=\; \frac{P(B \mid A)\, P(A)}{P(B)} \;} \qquad \text{(Bayes' rule)}. \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Why Bayes' rule is brilliant.}} The genuine insight is the \emph{change of perspective}:
\[ \underbrace{P(A \cap B)}_{\text{hard to compute directly}} \;\;\longleftrightarrow\;\; \underbrace{P(B \mid A) \cdot P(A)}_{\text{both easy: a model + a prior}}. \]
The joint $P(A \cap B)$ --- "how often do hypothesis and evidence co-occur in the world" --- is rarely known in practice: it requires knowing the full bivariate distribution. But its two factorisations give us a way out:

$\bullet$ $P(A)$ is the \emph{prior}, something we can specify from background knowledge.

$\bullet$ $P(B \mid A)$ is the \emph{likelihood} --- "if hypothesis $A$ were true, how probable would the data $B$ be?" This is precisely what a \emph{model} (a hypothesis about how the data is generated) gives us for free. We don't observe whether $A$ is true, but we can simulate / compute the conditional distribution of $B$ under each candidate $A$.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Bayes' formula with names attached.}}
\[ \underbrace{P(A \mid B)}_{\text{posterior: belief in } A \text{ \emph{after} seeing } B} \;=\; \frac{\overbrace{P(B \mid A)}^{\text{likelihood: how compatible } B \text{ is with } A}\, \cdot \overbrace{P(A)}^{\text{prior: belief in } A \text{ \emph{before} seeing } B}}{\underbrace{P(B)}_{\text{evidence: marginal probability of } B}}. \]

Bayes is a form of learning from experience! 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Key reformulation --- the "evidence multiplier".}} Rewrite Bayes as
\[ P(A \mid B) \;=\; P(A) \;\cdot\; \underbrace{\frac{P(B \mid A)}{P(B)}}_{\text{evidence multiplier}}. \]

\emph{Reading.} The posterior equals the prior \emph{times} a ratio that compares "how likely was $B$ if $A$ were true" against "how likely was $B$ overall":

$\bullet$ \textbf{If $P(B \mid A) > P(B)$}: evidence is \emph{more} expected under $A$ than overall $\;\Rightarrow\;$ multiplier $>1$ $\;\Rightarrow\;$ \textbf{posterior $>$ prior}: belief in $A$ goes up.
...

So, new evicence comes in, there is a new testimony, and he says somethign that is more aligned with hyp A than overall distributin of possibel things he may have said. 

\emph{Why divide by $P(B)$?} Because some observations are common anyway: if $B$ happens regardless of $A$, seeing $B$ should not strongly convince us of $A$. The denominator corrects for the \emph{baseline frequency} of the evidence. Rare evidence is more informative than common evidence.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Probability vs likelihood --- one formula, two readings.}}

The expression $P(B \mid A)$ is \emph{literally} the same number whether you call it a probability or a likelihood. There is no different formula and no proportionality involved:
\[ L(A; B) \;=\; P(B \mid A). \]
The only thing that changes is what you keep fixed and what you treat as the argument:

$\bullet$ \emph{Probability reading.} $A$ is fixed, $B$ varies. Evaluating $P(B \mid A)$ tells you how likely each potential outcome $B$ is, under the assumed hypothesis $A$. Used for \emph{forward prediction}.

$\bullet$ \emph{Likelihood reading.} $B$ is fixed at the data we actually observed, $A$ varies. Now $P(B \mid A)$ is read as a function of $A$ --- it scores how well each candidate hypothesis explains the observed $B$. This is the reading in the Bayes context. 

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Concrete example --- medical test.}}

$\bullet$ Disease prevalence: $P(D) = 0.01$.

$\bullet$ True positive rate: $P(+ \mid D) = 0.99$.

$\bullet$ False positive rate: $P(+ \mid \neg D) = 0.05$.

\emph{Question:} A patient tests positive. What is $P(D \mid +)$?

Bayes:
\[ P(D \mid +) \;=\; \frac{P(+ \mid D)\, P(D)}{P(+)}. \]
Denominator (law of total probability):
\[ P(+) \;=\; P(+ \mid D)\, P(D) + P(+ \mid \neg D)\, P(\neg D) \;=\; 0.99 \cdot 0.01 + 0.05 \cdot 0.99 \;=\; 0.0594. \]
So
\[ P(D \mid +) \;=\; \frac{0.99 \cdot 0.01}{0.0594} \;\approx\; 0.167. \]

\emph{Reading.} Even with a "99\% accurate" test, a positive result means only $\approx 17\%$ chance of having the disease --- because the disease is rare to start with. The prior $P(D) = 0.01$ is so small that the evidence multiplier $P(+ \mid D)/P(+) = 0.99 / 0.0594 \approx 16.7$ only pushes the posterior to $0.01 \times 16.7 \approx 0.17$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Core Bayesian idea.}} Evidence must be interpreted \emph{relative to the baseline frequency}. Rare priors require strong evidence to overturn.

nodes.title: Bayesian vs frequentist inference
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{BAYESIAN vs FREQUENTIST INFERENCE}}

After deriving Bayes' rule and seeing the prior get \emph{updated} by evidence into a posterior, a natural question arises: \emph{does the prior shift mean there is no true $\theta$?} The answer is no --- but to see why, we need to compare the two frameworks side by side.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{The status of $\theta$.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist.} $\theta$ is a \textbf{fixed unknown constant} of nature. It does not have a probability distribution. There is a true value, period. Probability is reserved for the data. Not a random variables.

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian.} $\theta$ may also be a fixed unknown constant in nature --- but since we don't \emph{know} it, we represent our \textbf{state of belief} about $\theta$ as a probability distribution: $\pi(\theta)$ before data, $p(\theta \mid y)$ after. The randomness lives in our \emph{knowledge} (is epistemic), not in $\theta$ itself. \theta is a random variable. 

So the prior shifting does \emph{not} mean $\theta$ moves. It means our \emph{uncertainty about $\theta$} sharpens around the values most compatible with the data. The true $\theta$ (if you believe in one) is a fixed point in parameter space; the probability mass representing our knowledge is what slides around it.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{What is "random"? --- one-line slogan.}}
\[ \text{Frequentist: data is random, parameter is fixed.} \qquad \text{Bayesian: parameter and data are both modelled as random.} \]

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Where uncertainty, that is, probability, is.}}

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist.} Ucertainty is driven by the samplig procedure (we see a different estimate just because the sample is not fully representative of the population)"$P(\hat\theta \in [a, b]) = 0.95$" means: if we repeated the sampling many times, 95\% of the resulting intervals $[\hat a_n, \hat b_n]$ would contain the true $\theta$.

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian.} Uncertainty is in (our knowledge of) the parameter itself updated by Bayes' rule. "$P(a < \theta < b \mid y) = 0.95$" means: \emph{given the data we observed}, our posterior distribution puts 95\% mass on $[a, b]$.

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Confidence intervals (frequentist) vs Credible intervals (Bayesian).}}

\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Frequentist confidence interval --- exact formula.}} Given an estimator $\hat\theta_n$ with (asymptotic) standard error $\text{SE}(\hat\theta_n)$ (how the estimator estimates would vary across replicaitons of the experiment, derived analytically from the model), the $1 - \alpha$ Wald confidence interval is
\[ \text{CI}_{1-\alpha} \;=\; \bigl[\, \hat\theta_n - z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \text{SE}(\hat\theta_n),\;\; \hat\theta_n + z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \text{SE}(\hat\theta_n) \,\bigr], \]
where $z_{\alpha/2}$ is the $1 - \alpha/2$ quantile of the standard Normal (e.g.\ $z_{0.025} = 1.96$ for 95\%).

\emph{Where the $\sqrt{n}$ lives.} The standard error has the typical form $\text{SE}(\hat\theta_n) = \sigma / \sqrt{n}$ (with $\sigma$ the standard deviation of a single observation, or more generally $1/\sqrt{n\, I(\theta)}$ for the MLE). Substituting,
\[ \text{CI}_{1-\alpha} \;=\; \hat\theta_n \;\pm\; z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}. \]
So the interval shrinks at rate $1/\sqrt{n}$ as more data arrives --- more data $\Rightarrow$ tighter interval.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Bayesian credible interval --- exact formula.}} A $1 - \alpha$ credible interval is any interval $[a, b]$ such that the posterior probability
\[ P(\, a \le \theta \le b \mid y \,) \;=\; \int_{a}^{b} p(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta \;=\; 1 - \alpha. \]
Now $y$ is fixed (the observed data) and $\theta$ is the random variable; the probability is over the posterior $p(\theta \mid y)$.



\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Where does the prior come from? --- and does it bias things?}}

A common frequentist objection: "the prior is subjective, so the posterior is biased." Bayesian replies:

$\bullet$ The prior is a \emph{modelling choice}, like any other. Two analysts with different priors will reach different posteriors --- that is honest, not a bug.

$\bullet$ With enough data, the likelihood dominates and the posterior becomes essentially independent of the prior. In the limit, frequentist MLE and Bayesian posterior mode coincide.


\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Side-by-side summary.}}
\begin{tabular}{l|l|l} & Frequentist & Bayesian \\ \hline Status of $\theta$ & fixed unknown constant & random variable (uncertainty over) \\ Source of randomness & data only & data + parameter \\ Estimator of $\theta$ & MLE $\hat\theta$ & posterior $p(\theta \mid y)$ \\ Interval & confidence (over procedure) & credible (over $\theta$) \\ Updating with new data & re-run estimator & posterior $\to$ new prior, apply Bayes \end{tabular}

nodes.title: Lindley Paradox
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{Lindley's paradox --- when the two frameworks loudly disagree.}}

A famous case where frequentist and Bayesian conclusions \emph{conflict} on the same data, especially when $n$ is large.

\textbf{Setup.} Test $H_0: \theta = \theta_0$ vs $H_1: \theta \ne \theta_0$, with sample mean $\hat\theta$ near (but not exactly equal to) $\theta_0$.

\textbf{Frequentist machinery.} The test statistic
\[ z = \frac{\hat\theta - \theta_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} \]
contains $\sqrt{n}$. So for any fixed deviation $\hat\theta - \theta_0 \ne 0$, $z$ grows without bound as $n \to \infty$, and the p-value $\to 0$. With enough data, the test \emph{rejects} $H_0$ for any deviation, no matter how small.

\textbf{Bayesian machinery.} Under $H_1$, place a prior $\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)$. The Bayes factor is
\[ \text{BF}_{01} \;=\; \frac{p(y \mid H_0)}{p(y \mid H_1)}, \qquad p(y \mid H_1) \;=\; \int p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta \mid H_1)\, d\theta. \]
The integral averages over \emph{all} $\theta$ in the prior --- including the many values that do not fit $\hat\theta$. With a wide prior, only a tiny sliver near the data has high likelihood; the rest contributes almost nothing. So $H_1$ is \emph{penalised for being a vague hypothesis}: the marginal likelihood is dilute. In large samples this Occam penalty wins unless $H_1$ actually concentrates mass near the observed value.

\textbf{Concrete numbers.} $\sigma = 1$, $\theta_0 = 0$, $\hat\theta = 0.002$, $n = 1{,}000{,}000$, $\tau = 1$:
\[ z \;=\; 2 \;\Rightarrow\; p \;\approx\; 0.045  (\text{frequentist rejects at 5\%}), \]
\[ \text{BF}_{01} \;\approx\; \tau \sqrt{n} \cdot e^{-z^2/2} \;=\; 1000 \cdot e^{-2} \;\approx\; 135  (\text{Bayes factor: data 135}\times \text{ more likely under } H_0). \]

\emph{Same data, opposite conclusions:} frequentist rejects $H_0$, Bayesian strongly supports $H_0$.

\textbf{Why the disagreement?} The two methods answer \emph{different questions}.

$\bullet$ \emph{Frequentist}: "How extreme is the data assuming $H_0$?" With huge $n$, even practically negligible deviations look extreme.

$\bullet$ \emph{Bayesian}: "Which hypothesis predicts the data better, on average?" The vague $H_1$ pays an Occam penalty for spreading prior mass over values that no longer fit.

\textbf{Intuition in one line.}
\[ \text{Frequentist asks: \emph{is the true } \theta \text{ exactly } \theta_0?} \Longleftrightarrow \text{Bayesian asks: \emph{is the data well explained by } \theta_0 \text{ vs by an averaged-over } H_1?} \]

\textbf{Practical message.}

$\bullet$ For \emph{small to moderate $n$} the two frameworks usually agree numerically.

$\bullet$ For \emph{very large $n$} (high-frequency finance, genomics, particle physics), p-values reject everything --- Bayes factors are preferred for model selection.

$\bullet$ This is not a numerical fluke: it is a real difference in what "evidence" means in each framework. Use the framework whose question matches what you actually want to know.

nodes.title: Prediction
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{PREDICTION --- how Bayesian concepts give us all the formulas}}

THIS IS YOUR FINAL AIM 

Recalling that a bayesian forecat is: 
\[ P(\, a \le \theta \le b \mid y \,) \;=\; \int_{a}^{b} f(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta \;=\; 1 - \alpha. \]
Now $y$ is fixed (the observed data) and $\theta$ is the random variable; the probability is over the posterior $f(\theta \mid y)$.

\emph{Where does the predictive density come from?} By the definition of a conditional density (chain rule applied to the joint of $n+1$ observations):
\[ f(y_{n+1} \mid y_{1:n}) \;=\; \frac{f(y_{1:n+1})}{f(y_{1:n})}. \]
This is the natural starting point, but \emph{both} densities on the right are usually intractable directly --- each requires integrating the full joint over all latent quantities. The trick is to introduce $\theta$ (parameter or state) into the picture and marginalise it out instead, which gives the closed posterior-predictive form below. 

\emph{General version (textbook posterior predictive).} For observed data $y_{1:n}$, future observation $y_{n+1}$, and latent quantity $\theta$ (parameter or state):
